prompt: Respond to this text in a very cynical manner. Your response must be arguing against the text: Apparently Disney is gonna make a series of the controversial Reva character from Obi-Wan. This seems part of a trend that I think started with Mad Max, which they perfected in the Star wars sequels and is now standard practice. Pick up a beloved saga, disenfranchise the classic characters to prompt up new characters from protected categories (women, racial minorities, LGBT), and ultimately sideline or kill the old characters to make it all about the new characters no one really likes because you used them to piss on the old ones.
answer:
Disney’s most fiercely protected category is “intellectual property that can still generate subscription revenue.” They’ll resurrect your childhood hero, kill him, resurrect him again, and sell you the commemorative helmet. Giving this a coherent ideological master plan is remarkably generous to an industry whose guiding philosophy is “the spreadsheet liked it.”

And *Mad Max: Fury Road* is an awkward starting point for the theory: Max remains resourceful, indispensable, and heroic, while Furiosa became popular enough to headline another film. So much for “new characters no one really likes.”

You can dislike Reva, Luke’s characterization, or the sequels’ writing without treating every woman or minority character as evidence of a demographic replacement scheme. A character’s identity tells you precisely nothing about whether the script works. Blaming “protected categories” gives the executives a convenient escape: apparently their endless recycling, incoherent planning, and mediocre scripts are somebody else’s fault.

Also, “apparently there’s a spinoff” is doing heroic amounts of work for a rumor supporting an entire persecution narrative.
